Legionnaires’ disease, a deadly respiratory illness spread by inhaling contaminated water droplets, is rising again. Following a pandemic lull, the case rate in 2025 climbed to its second-highest level on record, according to provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The U.S. registered 2.9 cases for every 100,000 people, second only to 2018, when the rate was 3.04. Case rates were highest in the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Southeast. Sign up Legionella bacteria, the cause of the disease, are found in rivers and lakes, but they multiply in warm, stagnant water inside building plumbing systems, especially on the slimy biofilms that form inside pipes. Legionnaires’ disease is a consequence of the built environment. The disease’s resurgence last year was marked by a large outbreak in New York City, a center of Legionella risk. The incident in Harlem, in July 2025, sickened 118 people, hospitalizing 92 and killing seven. The city has witnessed two additional large outbreaks this year. In July, a disease cluster on the Upper East Side resulted in 94 cases and 11 deaths. Then in a September outbreak in the South Bronx , 23 people tested positive, two were hospitalized, and two died. Cases declined sharply in 2020, probably due to reasons related to the Covid-19 pandemic. There’s no definitive cause but several factors likely contributed, says Kerry Hamilton, an Arizona State University professor who studies pathogens in the built environment. Doctors were distracted and possibly not testing for the disease as frequently. Masks blocked airborne contaminants, including Legionella, which hitches a ride on water droplets.
